blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A power-based sample size is the number of participants needed so that a planned comparison has a stated probability (the power, 1 − β) of giving a significant result at level α if the true effect equals a stated, clinically important size. It differs from the precision-based sample size of §7.3 (recall: n chosen so that one estimate has a stated margin of error). Estimating one prevalence needs §7.3; comparing groups, testing an association, or running a trial needs this section.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Sample size is a design decision, not a formula lookup. It starts with the primary research question, which fixes the primary outcome (what is measured) and the primary comparison (between which groups). Only then does “effect size” mean anything: the smallest difference that would matter clinically or for the programme, not the smallest that happens to be detectable. The remaining inputs (the expected variability or event rate, α and power; recall §8.4) are plugged into a formula that matches the planned analysis. A t-test, a comparison of proportions, a correlation and a log-rank test each have their own formula, which is why the analysis (recall §8.8) is chosen before the sample size.

All the formulas below come from one idea, derived in §8.4: the expected difference must lie (z_α/2 + z_β) standard errors from zero. With α = 0.05 two-sided and 80% power, z_α/2 = 1.960, z_β = 0.842, and (1.960 + 0.842)² = 7.849. For 90% power, z_β = 1.282 and the constant is 10.51.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Two means (recall §8.4). SE of the difference with n per group = σ√(2/n). Setting Δ/SE = z_α/2 + z_β gives

n per group = 2(z_α/2 + z_β)²σ² ÷ Δ².

Two proportions p₁, p₂. Under H₀ the difference has SE₀ = √(2p̄q̄/n), where p̄ = (p₁ + p₂)/2 and q̄ = 1 − p̄; under H₁ it has SE₁ = √[(p₁q₁ + p₂q₂)/n]. The test rejects when the observed difference exceeds z_α/2 × SE₀. Power is P(difference > z_α/2 SE₀) = Φ[(Δ − z_α/2 SE₀)/SE₁]. Setting this to 1 − β gives Δ = z_α/2 SE₀ + z_β SE₁. Multiply by √n and square:

n per group = [z_α/2 √(2p̄q̄) + z_β √(p₁q₁ + p₂q₂)]² ÷ (p₁ − p₂)².

Cohort study, via the risk ratio. Put p₀ = risk in the unexposed and p₁ = RR × p₀, then use the two-proportion formula.

Case-control study, via the odds ratio. The proportions compared are the proportions exposed among controls (p₀) and cases (p₁). The odds of exposure in cases are OR × p₀/(1 − p₀) (recall §10.6.4: the exposure OR equals the disease OR), so p₁ = OR × p₀ ÷ [1 + p₀(OR − 1)]. Then use the two-proportion formula.

Correlation. Fisher’s z = ½ ln[(1 + r)/(1 − r)] has SE 1/√(n − 3) (recall §11.2). Setting z(r)/SE = z_α/2 + z_β gives n = [(z_α/2 + z_β)/z(r)]² + 3.

Unequal allocation, k controls per case (or k:1 arms). The variance of a difference is σ²(1/n₁ + 1/n₂). With a fixed total N and n₂ = kn₁, n₁ = N/(1 + k), and the variance is σ²(1 + k)²/(kN). At 1:1 it is 4σ²/N. So k:1 needs (1 + k)²/(4k) times the total of a 1:1 design: 1.125 for 2:1, 1.33 for 3:1, 1.8 for 5:1. The inverse, 4k/(1 + k)², is the relative efficiency.

Cluster-randomised trial. Randomising clusters (villages, anganwadi centres) of m people each inflates the variance by the design effect 1 + (m − 1)ICC (recall §6.2.6 and §15.2.2), so multiply the individually randomised n by it and divide by m to get clusters per arm (Hayes & Bennett, 1999).

Survival (events-driven). For a log-rank test or Cox model with a proportion a allocated to one arm, the number of events needed is D = (z_α/2 + z_β)² ÷ [a(1 − a)(ln HR)²], which is 4(z_α/2 + z_β)²/(ln HR)² for 1:1 allocation (Schoenfeld, 1983; derivation beyond this book; not to be confused with the Schoenfeld residuals of §14.6.2). Power depends on events, not people. The number to enrol is D divided by the expected proportion who will have the event during follow-up.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Five planning questions from one district, each at α = 0.05 (two-sided) and 80% power.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Two means. Iron–folic acid with counselling is expected to raise mean haemoglobin in anaemic adolescent girls by 0.5 g/dL; SD 1.2 g/dL. n = 2 × 7.849 × 1.2² ÷ 0.5² = 2 × 7.849 × 1.44 ÷ 0.25 = 90.4 → 91 per group (92 by the t-distribution, which software computes).
  2. Two proportions. Peer counselling is expected to raise exclusive breastfeeding at 6 months from 40% to 55%. p̄ = 0.475. √(2 × 0.475 × 0.525) = 0.7062; √(0.40 × 0.60 + 0.55 × 0.45) = 0.6982. n = (1.960 × 0.7062 + 0.8416 × 0.6982)² ÷ 0.15² = (1.3842 + 0.5876)² ÷ 0.0225 = 3.888 ÷ 0.0225 = 172.8 → 173 per group.
  3. Case-control. Not-EBF is expected in 30% of controls; the smallest OR worth detecting is 2. p₁ = 2 × 0.30 ÷ (1 + 0.30) = 0.4615. The two-proportion formula gives 140.7 → 141 cases and 141 controls.
  4. Cohort. Diarrhoea risk in exclusively breastfed infants 20%; RR to detect 1.5, so p₁ = 0.30. n = 293.2 → 294 per group.
  5. Correlation. To detect r = 0.30 between years of service and anganwadi workers’ knowledge scores: z(0.30) = ½ ln(1.3/0.7) = 0.3095. n = (2.802/0.3095)² + 3 = 81.9 + 3 = 84.9 → 85 workers.
  6. Cluster RCT. Question 2 run by randomising anganwadi centres, 20 infants per centre, ICC 0.05 from earlier surveys. DEFF = 1 + 19 × 0.05 = 1.95. n = 172.8 × 1.95 = 337.0 per arm → 337/20 = 16.9 → 17 centres per arm (340 infants).
  7. Events-driven. A CBHI retention intervention should cut the dropout hazard by 30% (HR 0.70). D = 4 × 7.849 ÷ (ln 0.70)² = 31.40 ÷ 0.1272 = 246.8 → 247 dropouts. If 30% of households are expected to drop out during follow-up, enrol 246.8/0.30 = 822.6 → 823 households.
  8. Unequal allocation. Question 1 with 2:1 allocation and the same 182 girls: the variance rises by 9/8, so Δ/SE falls from 2.802 to 2.802/√1.125 = 2.641, and power = Φ(2.641 − 1.960) = Φ(0.681) = 0.75, not 0.80. Keeping 80% needs the unrounded 1:1 total, 2 × 90.4 = 180.8, times 1.125 = 203.4: 68 + 136 = 204 girls.
  9. Losses. Inflate the final n for expected loss to follow-up exactly as for non-response (recall §7.3): 91 per group with 15% expected loss becomes 91/0.85 = 107.1 → 108 per group.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(pwr)
power.t.test(delta = 0.5, sd = 1.2, power = 0.80)$n        # two means
# two proportions
power.prop.test(p1 = 0.40, p2 = 0.55, power = 0.80)$n
# case-control, OR 2
power.prop.test(p1 = 0.30, p2 = 0.4615, power = 0.80)$n
# correlation
pwr.r.test(r = 0.3, power = 0.80)$n
z <- qnorm(0.975) + qnorm(0.80)
# events for HR 0.7
4 * z^2 / log(0.7)^2
# power, 2:1 at the 1:1 total
pnorm(z / sqrt(9/8) - qnorm(0.975))
[1] 91.38944
[1] 172.7999
[1] 140.7206
[1] 84.07364
[1] 246.7871
[1] 0.7521895

Line by line: 91.4 (step 1, by the t-distribution, so 92 per group); 172.8 (step 2, the same formula as the Derivation); 140.7 (step 3); 84.1 (step 5; pwr.r.test adds a small-sample correction, and both round up to 85); 246.8 events (step 7); and power 0.752 for 2:1 allocation (step 8). Every n is rounded up.

points.html: Inputs, not outputs. n depends on α, power, the effect size and the variability or baseline risk (recall §8.4). The effect size is the smallest important effect, not the effect you hope for or found in a small pilot.
Halving Δ quadruples n. Every formula has Δ² (or (ln HR)², or z(r)²) in the denominator.

Clustering must be planned for. Omitting the design effect when clusters are randomised or sampled gives a trial whose effective sample size is DEFF times smaller than planned, so it is underpowered. With few clusters per arm, the analysis needs small-sample care (recall §15.2.5).
Unequal allocation costs little until it is extreme. 2:1 needs 12.5% more participants; 3:1, 33% more.
Survival studies are sized in events. A long follow-up or a higher-risk population reaches the events sooner.
Report the calculation with every input and its source, so a reader can reproduce n (CONSORT, the trial reporting guideline of §15.9, asks for this).
After the study, report the estimate and its CI, not “observed power” (recall §8.4). An underpowered study cannot be rescued by reanalysis.

questions.prompt: A trial was sized at 91 girls per arm for 80% power with 1:1 allocation. For recruitment reasons the investigators switch to 2:1 (intervention:control) but keep the same total of 182. Compute the relative efficiency and the new power. How many girls would 2:1 need to keep 80% power?
questions.answer: For k:1 allocation the variance of the difference is (1 + k)²/(4k) times that of 1:1 at the same total. For k = 2: 9/8 = 1.125, so the relative efficiency is 8/9 = 0.889 (11% information lost). At 1:1, Δ/SE = z_α/2 + z_β = 1.960 + 0.842 = 2.802. At 2:1 it falls to 2.802/√1.125 = 2.641. Power = Φ(2.641 − 1.960) = Φ(0.681) = 0.75, down from 0.80: a modest loss. To keep 80% power: 180.8 × 1.125 = 203.4 → n₁ = 67.8 → 68 and n₂ = 135.6 → 136, 204 girls in all (about 22 more).

questions.prompt: A calculation gives 200 per group, but 20% loss to follow-up is expected. What should the enrolment target be, and why is 200 × 1.2 slightly wrong?
questions.answer: Enrol n/(1 − loss) = 200/0.80 = 250 per group, so that 80% of 250 = 200 complete the study. 200 × 1.2 = 240 would leave only 0.80 × 240 = 192, below the required 200. The calculated n assumes complete data on everyone analysed.

questions.prompt: A cohort study will compare 1-year diarrhoea risk in infants of mothers with and without a latrine at home. Risk without a latrine is 15%; the smallest important difference is a fall to 10%. Compute n per group for 80% power at α = 0.05, and then allow for 10% loss to follow-up.
